summary.text:
Babergh's 2026/27 Joint Capital, Investment and Treasury Management Strategy pack (report MC/25/39), taken to Babergh Full Council on 24 February and Mid Suffolk Full Council on 26 February 2026. Prepared jointly with Mid Suffolk District Council (separate GSS E07000203) — every substantive table splits the two councils. Adviser: Arlingclose. Second read for E07000200: the H1 2025/26 report (MC/25/30) was read earlier and sits at papers/E07000200/40782.txt.

Position at 31 March 2026 forecast: total external borrowing £131.639m — PWLB £86.139m, existing short-term £13.000m, new short-term (planned Q4 2025/26 drawdown) £32.500m. Held flat at £131.639m through 2027/28 then rises £4m/year to £143.639m by 2030/31. CFR £181.955m at 31 March 2026 forecast, rising modestly to £183.259m at 31 March 2027 budget and £182.640m by 2030/31. Implied internal borrowing £50.3m (2025/26 fc) — the paper does not print internal borrowing as a standalone Babergh line but the balance-sheet identity closes to £127k against the Liability Benchmark Usable Reserves line, so the identity holds. No other long-term liabilities disclosed anywhere in the paper.

Loan-book reconciliation does not tie. Their Chart 1 prints PWLB £86.139m at 31 March 2026 forecast; our price_book.py as-at snapshot returns 6 live loans totalling £91.122m at 3.39% weighted — £4.98m above their reported PWLB. Same shape and size of gap as the H1 read. The likely culprit is the £11m loan ref 913286 (a legacy 6-digit reference, rate 77bp above the book weighted) — most probably prepaid or refinanced and not dropped from our file. Same 'Start-field drift' family as Cambridge (E07000008) and Canterbury (E07000106). Under current pipeline guidance the loan-book claim is left out of the email entirely and the draft is written from everything else the paper gives.

Three treasury-side hooks the email is built on. First and primary: the maturity profile. Appendix D on page 36 puts 35% of Babergh's fixed-rate book inside 12 months against a 50% upper limit — c£46m rolling — and Chart 1 on page 22 decomposes it neatly as £13m existing short-term plus £32.5m new short-term planned in Q4. The Borrowing Strategy paragraphs on page 26 explain the rate reasoning (short below long, so short-term or internal preferred). Between the December 2025 forecast the strategy was set against and today, Bank Rate has not moved — Arlingclose expected 3.25% by mid-2026, actual is still 3.75%. Short/long spread has narrowed but not closed. Second: the liability benchmark. Table 4 on page 24 climbs £155.4m (26/27) → £171.2m (30/31) while planned external debt sits at £131.6m rising to £143.6m — internal borrowing carries £24m of the gap at the front of the MTFP growing to £28m, funded from usable reserves falling £50m to £24m. Third and secondary: the MRP annuity method for post-2008 GF borrowing at Appendix G paragraph 1.5 uses 'the average PWLB annuity rate for the year of expenditure' — a rate we publish daily. Same hook shape as Tower Hamlets.

What is not raised: our loan-book figures (reconciliation fails); the 5.5x jump in the 1% interest-rate risk indicator (methodology change per §1.3, not real exposure change); the CIFCO yield divergence (Babergh 0.79% vs Mid Suffolk 1.25% on the same 50/50 holding — internal accounting difference); the Babergh Growth Ltd £3m ECL vs £938k reserve (their disclosure); LOBOs (none for Babergh — the £4m book sits entirely with Mid Suffolk); the investment yield collapse (7.94% → 3.0% baked out — paper has already made the observation itself). Meeting is six months past; there is no fixed upcoming Babergh treasury meeting to write ahead of, so send_by targets the typical mid-late 2026 annual outturn window.

Officer contacts named on the front sheet: Melissa Evans, Director, Finance and Procurement (confirmed S151 at App C §4.6 p29); David Feveyear-Ward, Head of Finance. NO email addresses are printed anywhere in the paper. Same as H1. Draft is prepared as 'drafted — needs an address'.

officer.body:
Dear Melissa,

Apologies for the cold email. PWLBtoday is fairly new so you may not have come across us yet.

We're built for local authority treasury teams and nothing else: live PWLB rates at both daily fixings, a monthly breakdown of every loan the sector draws, every council's PWLB book priced daily against the DMO's repayment curve, and a training academy for officers and members. There's more — the predictor, the SONIA path, peer metrics, a daily brief — in the brochure at [BROCHURE URL]. We don't sell treasury products, and the data side is free and stays free.

To keep the data and the training relevant we built tools that watch committee papers across every council in the country, so we can see how a council's own figures compare with where the market has gone since the strategy was set. So below are a couple of thoughts on the Joint Capital, Investment and Treasury Management Strategies pack (MC/25/39) approved on 24 and 26 February. You're not being singled out — every authority gets one of these — and there's no agenda in it. It's a clearly laid out paper and this is offered in that spirit, not as a critique.

The thing that reads sharpest is the maturity profile. Appendix D on page 36 puts 35% of Babergh's borrowing book inside twelve months — the largest single bucket, and with 15 points of headroom against the 50% upper limit. Chart 1 on page 22 decomposes it: £13m of existing short-term borrowing plus £32.5m of new short-term drawn in Q4 2025/26, together about £46m rolling within the year. Your Borrowing Strategy paragraphs on page 26 explain the reasoning — short rates below long rates, so short or internal preferred — and that logic is arguably stronger now than when it was written. Arlingclose's December forecast on page 40 had Bank Rate down to 3.25% by mid-2026; on 14 August's PM fixing Bank Rate is still 3.75%, so the roll-out cost of that £46m is running about half a point above the forecast the budget was set against. On the same fixing PWLB Certainty rates at longer maturities sit at 5.34% at 5 years, 5.83% at 10, 6.38% at 20 and 6.27% at 50 — the long end has moved up since December, which widens rather than closes the short/long spread the strategy leans on.

The other reading is the shape of your liability benchmark. Table 4 on page 24 climbs from £155.4m in 2026/27 to £171.2m by 2030/31, while planned external debt sits flat at £131.6m through 2027/28 and rises to £143.6m by 2030/31. That is roughly £24m of internal borrowing carrying the difference at the front of the MTFP, growing to £28m by the end — funded from usable reserves that the same table shows falling from £50m to £24m. It's a coherent plan and it's what the LB is supposed to reveal. The useful thing is watching where the reserves thin enough that some of the £24-28m has to fund itself externally instead.

We price every published council's PWLB book daily against the DMO's premature-repayment curve at pwlbtoday.org/loan-analysis, and the liability benchmark pathway sits interactive at pwlbtoday.org/pwlb-activity — with CIPFA's forthcoming Prudential and Treasury Code updates it becomes central for everyone, and an interactive version lets you stress the reserves path directly.

On training, three fit the paper. "Refinancing risk and rolling short-term maturity" picks up the £46m rolling position and the Q4 drawdown decision. "Liability Benchmark: using it in practice" sits directly on Table 4. "MRP — policy options and revenue impact" covers Appendix G, where the post-2008 MRP schedule references the average PWLB annuity rate for the year of expenditure — that is a rate we publish daily. All 115 courses are free to local authorities until the end of September at pwlbtoday.org/academy, and free accounts for the whole team.

And if any of it is useful, mentioning it to others would help us more than anything. We're small, word of mouth is most of our marketing, and every sign-up helps us prove the need.

Sign up free → https://pwlbtoday.org/
Follow on LinkedIn → https://www.linkedin.com/company/pwlbtoday/

Russell
